Moldovan president, at NATO Parliamentary Assembly, says Russia wages two wars – one conventional against Ukraine, another cognitive war against European democracies, NATO countries
articles.body: Moldovan president, at NATO Parliamentary Assembly, says Russia wages two wars – one conventional against Ukraine, another cognitive war against European democracies, NATO countries Russia is waging two mutually reinforcing wars: one conventional war against Ukraine and one cognitive war against European democracies and NATO countries. President Maia Sandu today made statements to this effect in her speech at the annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin. “The first is the conventional war against Ukraine, fought with missiles, drones, and artillery to seize territory and deprive a nation of its freedom. The second is a cognitive war against the democracies of Europe and the NATO area – a war meant to change what people believe, what they fear, whom they trust and ultimately the decisions they make,” the head of state said. “Russia does not need to defeat Europe’s armies, if it can undermine the political will behind them.” The president described how this war operates, drawing on the experience of Moldova. At the recent elections, Russia spent the equivalent of approximately 2 per cent of Moldova’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on vote-buying, illegal party financing, cyberattacks, false bomb alerts at polling stations abroad and coordinated online campaigns. “Our citizens defended their choice and our institutions held firm,” Maia Sandu emphasized. The head of state also spoke about Russian drones violating the airspace of Moldova – more than 80 incidents involving drones and other aerial threats in 2026, each followed by information manipulation. “First, they make people feel unsafe. Then they try to convince them that defending themselves is even more dangerous,” the Moldovan president said. Maia Sandu warned countries preparing for elections that protecting the electoral process must begin well before the campaign. “Elections are the moment when people turn their beliefs, fears and perceptions into decisions. And Russia may have spent years shaping them,” Maia Sandu said. Drawing on the lessons learned by Moldova, the head of state proposed five directions for responding to Russia’s cognitive warfare: “Moldova is constitutionally neutral. But neutrality does not mean weakness, indifference to the brutal aggression against a neighbor or having to face security threats alone,” the President said. She noted that Moldova contributed to regional security as a stable and friendly neighbor of Ukraine and through its participation in the NATO mission in Kosovo and the European Union (EU) mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Moldovan president emphasized that joining the European Union meant securing a future of peace and freedom for Moldova, consolidating democracy and strengthening security. The head of state reiterated the goal of concluding accession negotiations by 2028, noting that four negotiating clusters had been opened and that the country was also prepared to open the remaining two. During the session, President Maia Sandu was presented with the NATO Parliamentary Assembly’s, Women for Peace and Security Award. Moldova has been a NATO partner since 1994. Cooperation focuses on modernizing defense institutions, resilience and cybersecurity, while respecting the country’s constitutional neutrality. articles.summary: Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China
articles.body: Tajikistan has now become the fourth country to announce its formal withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, Netherlands since the US announced its intention to "dismantle" the body — joining Chad, Naoero [formerly Nauru] and Venezuela. US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have railed against the court as abusing its jurisdiction, with Trump publicly attacking the ICC during remarks at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — who is wanted by the court for war crimes committed during the course of Russia's full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine . Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China. The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, crimes of aggression and war crimes in instances when national cannot or will not act. The ICC issued an international arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023. Tajikistan 's government said it made the decision to initiate the one-year withdrawal process on Friday, when Putin made a stopover visit after leaving his trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi. The ICC said it "regrets" Tajikistan's decision, adding that the move undermines "the collective pursuit of justice" and weakens "global efforts to end impunity." "The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community," an ICC statement continued. Tajikistan signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC back in 1998 and ratified it in 2000. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have also announced their withdrawal from the court, blasting it as a tool of "neocolonial repression." articles.title: Zelenskyy calls for talks with Russia 'as soon as possible'
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia to begin as soon as possible
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia – and involving European countries – to begin as soon as possible.

"We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting – Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia – happens as soon as possible," he told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link.

"We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas," he said. "We hope it happens sooner. We are ready to do this literally tomorrow."

Iran war dominates Qatar-US talks in Washington, DC
articles.body:
The US-Israel war on Iran was part of the agenda at the meeting between Qatar’s prime minister and the US secretary of state in Washington, DC.

They released a joint statement saying both sides reaffirmed their commitment to upholding freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

They stressed that safety and unimpeded passage through this vital waterway are essential to regional security, reliable energy supplies and global economic stability.

Earlier this month, Qatar’s PM met US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at the White House.

After that meeting, Trump said that the conflict appeared to be effectively coming to an end, and Qatar’s PM described that conversation as being a positive one.

But at the end of the day, there was no significant breakthrough in coming to a peace deal to end this war, and most recently, we’re now hearing reports of strikes in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Yemen’s government accuses Houthis of deadly attacks on civilians
articles.summary: Yemen’s internationally recognised government has strongly condemned what it says were Houthi attacks on civilians in Lahj and Aden
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has strongly condemned what it says were Houthi attacks on civilians in Lahj and Aden.

The Human Rights Ministry said four civilians were killed and 10 others were injured in the district of al-Maqatirah in the governorate of Lahj after passenger buses and commercial trucks were hit by Houthi shelling today.

The ministry also condemned a Houthi drone attack in the al-Buraiqah district in the governorate of Aden, which it says killed three children and injured seven other civilians.

It urged the international community to help protect civilians and called for aid to be allowed into the besieged city of Taiz.

articles.title: Iran’s chief negotiator says stalemate in war ‘must be resolved’
articles.body:
Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says Tehran will not let the US impose its “no war, no peace” objectives on the country.

Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reports Ghalibaf said the situation “cannot continue… and must be resolved”.

“The question now is how, by whom, and with what actions should we resolve this situation.”

articles.title: Qatar PM’s visit to Washington part of attempt to revive US-Iran ceasefire talks
articles.body:
The negotiations between Qatar’s prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, are part of a series of talks by the Qataris to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war on Iran.

Even if it may not lead to a big breakthrough today, the goal is to at least get the discussions going between Tehran and Washington.

But tensions have been escalating, with US President Donald Trump saying over the weekend that he was inclined to start military strikes on Iran after the new year if no deal is reached. He also said he wanted a permanent agreement that will stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons, and called Iranian officials “very difficult”.

This meeting comes after Qatari mediators met Iranian officials in Germany for a two-hour discussion on possible diplomatic efforts.

Iran is pressuring Washington to accept a two-day proposal that would ease the economic sanctions on Iran, lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports, in exchange for the Strait of Hormuz reopening. But US Secretary of State Rubio says those terms are unacceptable, unreasonable and unrealistic.

But the fact that the meeting is still happening shows there may be a path forward to finding a way to end this war.

Reports: Russia planning to station nuclear weapon in space
articles.body:
Western military intelligence services believe Russia is planning to station a nuclear weapon in space by the end of this year, German media reported on Monday morning.

According to public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche Zeitung broadsheet, intelligence chiefs believe Moscow intends to fire a satellite armed with a nuclear warhead into orbit.

Intelligence regarding the plans was reportedly shared among NATO member states recently and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is said to have been informed by experts from Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr.

A Bundeswehr spokesman reportedly declined to comment on the reports, acknowledging only that Russia does possess such capabilities and warning that a nuclear explosion in space would have devastating consequences for global satellite communications.

"It would effectively mean: back to the stone age," he said.

The German Ministry of Defense said only that it was continuously observing global developments in space while the Russian embassy in Berlin said it had no information regarding such plans.

The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) warned in October that Russia was developing a satellite capable of transporting a nuclear weapon and, according to the new report, a satellite codenamed "Sputnik-S" is believed to have been in storage in the Moscow area for several years.

Back in February 2022, the same month as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia launched its "Kosmos-2552" satellite into orbit, considered by western intelligence at the time to be a test designed to measure the effects of radiation in space.

Should Moscow indeed launch a nuclear weapon into space, it would constitute a breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty which prohibits the stationing of weapons of mass destructions in Earth orbit. Russia agreed to a continuation of the treaty at the United Nations General Assembly in December 2024.

Space is nevertheless becoming increasingly militarized, with the United States admitting in September 2025 that it had positioned offensive non-nuclear weapons in orbit.

articles.summary: The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has signed an order on the conscription of citizens for compulsory active military service and the transfer of servicemen completing their compulsory service to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027. The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan. Under the order, citizens of Azerbaijan born in 2009 who have reached the age of 18 by the date of conscription (inclusive), as well as those born between 1997 and 2008 who are under the age of 30, have not completed compulsory active military service in the Azerbaijani Armed Forces, and are not entitled to deferment or exemption from conscription, will be called up for compulsory active military service from January 1 through 30, 2027. Servicemen who have completed the service period stipulated in Article 38.1.1 of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan "On Military Duty and Military Service" will be transferred to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027. The Cabinet of Ministers of Azerbaijan is tasked with taking the measures provided for by law to implement this order.

articles.title: Ademovic: The Constitutional Court of BiH is the only bulwark against the Secessionist Policy of the RS
articles.summary: This assessment was offered by Nedim Ademović—a lawyer and expert in constitutional law—during the Dnevnik 2 news program on Federal Television
articles.body: The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina remains the only state-level institution with the capacity to halt actions that threaten the sovereignty, independence, and functionality of the state. This assessment was offered by Nedim Ademović—a lawyer and expert in constitutional law—during the Dnevnik 2 news program on Federal Television. He was commenting on recent rulings by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, political rhetoric emanating from the Republika Srpska (RS), and announcements that the formation of government at the state level would be made conditional upon certain demands. Ademović warns that the Constitutional Court is currently under fire precisely because of its role in upholding the constitutional order, and that any potential reforms aimed at limiting its functionality would pose a serious risk to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He argues that pro-Bosnian political forces must begin considering various scenarios now and focus on safeguarding the institutional capacity of this body. Constitutional Court Rulings on the Commission and Symbols of the Army of the RBiH Were Expected Addressing the Constitutional Court’s rulings—which concerned a veto exercised by Željka Cvijanović regarding the Commission to Preserve National Monuments, as well as an attempt to criminalize the display of symbols associated with the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina—Ademović characterized these actions by the authorities in the Republika Srpska as unconstitutional. “In my view, these are blatantly unconstitutional acts by the RS, which continue to attempt to weaken the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its institutions, and its functionality. These rulings are significant because such acts are being eliminated from the constitutional and legal framework of our state. Nevertheless, given that these are blatantly unconstitutional decisions, they were the only ones to be expected,” said Ademović. He pointed out that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has demonstrated that it is the only state institution capable of functioning independently and halting moves that threaten the sovereignty and independence of the state. Explaining the decision regarding the Commission to Preserve National Monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ademović stated that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted the decision to appoint members of the Commission by a majority vote; however, Željka Cvijanović attempted to invoke an “entity veto”—facilitated by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska—to overturn it. “The Constitutional Court ruled that this was not permissible, for the simple reason that an entity veto cannot be used indiscriminately; it may only be applied in relation to five specific competencies defined by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The ruling is logical and straightforward. It now paves the way for this vital commission to finally become functional again, after so many years,” Ademović clarified. Commenting on a statement by Savo Minić—a representative of Republika Srpska—that a state-level government cannot be formed without first resolving issues concerning the Office of the High Representative (OHR), state property, and the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ademović highlighted the Court’s critical role in upholding the constitutional order. “For Republika Srpska – on its radical, secessionist path – the Constitutional Court stands as the sole institution that truly serves as a bulwark against such a policy. Unlike other institutions – such as the state-level legislative body or the Council of Ministers – the Constitutional Court is not subject to vetoes, ethnic quotas, or specific majority requirements. Instead, it reaches decisions by a simple majority vote, just like any other court in Europe,” said Ademović. He added that this is the only institution with the capacity to declare certain acts unconstitutional – a step that, as he noted, opens the door for the international community to take action, including political and other measures, to halt the moves made by the authorities of the Republika Srpska (RS). “I still believe that the RS, as an entity, is stronger than Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of de facto power. However, without the Constitutional Court, they might be able to exercise that de facto power. With the Constitutional Court in place, that is impossible, because there is always a document on the table that spells out what they are doing right and what they are doing wrong,” Ademović pointed out. According to him, it is precisely for this reason that the RS authorities are seeking to reform the Constitutional Court in a way that would render it dysfunctional – mirroring the blocking mechanisms already present in other state institutions. Warning Regarding Potential Reforms Reflecting on the international landscape and the efforts of the Republika Srpska (RS) authorities to achieve their political objectives, Ademović pointed to the passivity of the European Union, as well as shifts in international relations. “Global circumstances – specifically the relationship with the United States and the RS’s active engagement with that country, the passivity of the European Union (another key player), and the situation in our immediate neighborhood – are currently not particularly conducive to upholding the functionality and prosperity of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Ademović assessed. He believes it is time to sound the alarm, noting that key reforms in Bosnia and Herzegovina since the Dayton Peace Agreement came into effect have largely been the result of international community involvement or pressure exerted on domestic political actors by third parties. He warned that, under these conditions, room could open up for a compromise involving the reform of the Constitutional Court – a move that would undermine its functionality. “Circumstances could align in such a way that pressure is applied once again, leading to concessions – specifically, a compromise involving the reform of the Constitutional Court. We must be extremely cautious here. The Constitutional Court, as a functional institution that defends this state, must remain functional – exactly as it is. We must not allow the introduction of elements that have compromised other institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina—such as requirements for the mandatory presence of a specific number of representatives from certain ethnic groups to establish a quorum or make decisions,” Ademović stated. He concluded that pro-Bosnian forces face a serious task and must begin developing possible options for a potential reform of the Constitutional Court – ensuring, however, that the institution retains the functionality and capacities it possesses today, Federalna writes.

articles.title: Under new draft constitution, Constitutional Court may ban political party activities in Armenia November 23, 13:31
articles.summary: The new draft constitution stipulates that the governing bodies of parties in Armenia should be formed through elections
articles.body: The draft of the new constitution of Armenia includes a separate chapter dedicated to political parties and the media, emphasizing their important role in the life of a democratic state. The new draft constitution stipulates that the governing bodies of parties in Armenia should be formed through elections. This enables party members to participate in the running of the party and ensures the maintenance of democratic principles within the parties as well. Parties in Armenia must operate on the principle of financial transparency so that it is clear to the public where they receive their funding. They can receive donations from individuals, as well as be financed from the state budget in cases prescribed by law. The goal is to ensure fair political competition and increase public trust in parties. Also, the proposed constitution underscores the free expression of the will of voters and its protection. Parties should not influence citizens' choices through bribery, pressure, or other impermissible means. The draft stipulates that the Constitutional Court of Armenia may prohibit the activities of a party in the country if it is aimed at undermining the free will of voters, the party has received foreign funding, or advocates the rejection of Armenia’s independence. The media in Armenia also are required to have financial transparency so that the public is informed about their financing. Thus, the draft of the new constitution of Armenia assigns an important place to parties and the media in a democratic society, while emphasizing the principles of their uninhibited activity, financial transparency, and accountability.

Serbia’s Student Movement Criticises European Parliament’s Vukovar Resolution
articles.summary: It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia
articles.body: Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won the country’s recent parliamentary elections, has criticised a European Parliament’s draft resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, calling for adequate recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict. In a statement on the Student List – Students Win website on Monday, it said the resolution does not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation. It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia, including killings, persecution and mass displacement, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995. “Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the students said. “Serbia has an obligation to cooperate in clarifying the fate of missing persons and establishing responsibility for crimes committed, but the same approach must also apply to Serb victims and crimes committed against them,” the student movement said. The eastern border town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serb paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, during the war in Croatia, after which the remaining population was expelled. Two days after the town fell, Croatian prisoners and civilians were taken from Vukovar Hospital to a nearby farm where at least 200 people were executed. The student movement warned that remembrance of the past should not deepen existing divisions in the region. “True reconciliation cannot be achieved by imposing one-sided interpretations of the past, but through an honest reckoning with all crimes, regardless of who committed them or against whom,” they added. The European Parliament was set to debate the resolution on Monday, with a vote scheduled for Thursday. The debate in Strasbourg follows the submission of two motions for a resolution on November 20, commemorating the victims of the siege of Vukovar and the atrocities that followed. One of the motions, submitted by members of the European People’s Party, EPP, the Socialists and Democrats, S&D, the European Conservatives and Reformists, ECR, and the Greens/EFA, notes that 1,725 cases of missing persons from the war remain unresolved, including 1,341 people whose fate remains unknown and 384 whose deaths have been confirmed but whose burial sites have yet to be located. It also calls on Serbia to grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose information about the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for war crimes and facilitate the identification and return of victims’ remains to their families. The proposal further urges Serbia to adopt its long-announced law on missing persons. The motion condemns the denial and glorification of war crimes, specifically referring to the public honours paid in Serbia to the convicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in September 2026. It further calls for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims. The proposal acknowledges the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, ITCY, for the former Yugoslavia in prosecuting crimes committed in Vukovar, but adds that not all those responsible have been brought to justice. The motion also highlights the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Croatian into Croatia in 1998 as an example of successful post-war reintegration and the importance of rebuilding trust between communities.

articles.title: Four Cantons constituting their Assemblies Today, electing Leaderships
articles.summary: The constitutive sessions of the assemblies of the Herzegovina-Neretva, Central Bosnia, Posavina, and West Herzegovina Cantons are taking place today
articles.body: The constitutive sessions of the assemblies of the Herzegovina-Neretva, Central Bosnia, Posavina, and West Herzegovina Cantons are taking place today. In addition to confirming mandates, the representatives will elect the assembly leadership and delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH). The session of the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton Assembly begins at 11:00 a.m. in Mostar. Following the verification of the elected representatives’ mandates, the agenda includes the formation of caucuses for the constituent peoples, the election of the Assembly Speaker (or Deputy Speaker), and the election of delegates to the FBiH Parliament’s House of Peoples. The constitutive session of the Central Bosnia Canton Assembly—which consists of 30 representatives—will be held in Travnik. The SDA and HDZ BiH hold a majority, with 19 seats between them. The agenda includes the acceptance of mandates, the formation of temporary working bodies (such as the Commission for Selection and Appointments), and the election of the Assembly leadership and delegates to the FBiH House of Peoples. Negotiations regarding the formation of a new cantonal government have not yet begun. The Posavina Canton Assembly will be constituted in Domaljevac. Representatives will receive their certificates of mandate, followed by the taking of a formal oath. The agenda includes the election of the Mandate and Immunity Commission and the Commission for Selection and Appointments, the formation of caucuses for the constituent peoples, the election of the Assembly leadership, and the selection of delegates to the FBiH Parliament’s House of Peoples. In the new composition, the HDZ BiH holds 13 seats, the SDA holds three, while the other parties and lists have won one seat each. The constitutive session of the Assembly of the West Herzegovina Canton is taking place in Široki Brijeg. In the new composition, the HDZ BiH holds 17 seats; the HDZ 1990–HSS and the Croatian Republican Party (Hrvatska republikanska stranka) hold two seats each; while the HSP BiH and the coalition of the HSP Dr. Ante Starčević BiH and the HSP BiH of Herceg-Bosna each have one representative. Following the election of delegates to the House of Peoples of the FBiH, the process of forming the Government of the West Herzegovina Canton is expected to begin.

articles.title: Igor Dodik Prime Minister-Designate for the Composition of the New RS Government
articles.summary: Igor Dodik said he accepts the mandate with full responsibility towards Republika Srpska and all its citizens
articles.body: On Sunday, after consulting with coalition partners, the President of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian entity Republika Srpska, Savo Minić, announced that he proposed Igor Dodik as the prime Minister-Designate for the new Government of Republika Srpska. Igor Dodik said he accepts the mandate with full responsibility towards Republika Srpska and all its citizens. “We will get to work and prove that Republika Srpska knows how to and can win on all fronts,” he said. He emphasized that it is a great honor, that people have placed their trust in him, and that he bears a huge responsibility. “We are aware that only a strong economy and institutions give us the freedom to independently make decisions about how we want our children to grow up, in what kind of environment, who we cooperate with, and who we want to represent us,” Dodik added. Minić said that the new government will be quickly formed and that it will be the government of continuity. Previously, Minić held consultations with representatives of political parties regarding the selection of the prime minister designate. In separate meetings on Sunday, he held consultations with representatives of the ruling coalition parties. According to the Constitution of Republika Srpska, the president of Republika Srpska proposes to the National Assembly a candidate for the vice-president of the Government, and the National Assembly of Republika Srpska must confirm the candidate. Igor Dodik is the Organizational Secretary of the SNSD and the son of the party’s president, Milorad Dodik. In the general elections in October, he ran for the National Assembly of Republika Srpska for the first time, and according to the preliminary results, he won the highest number of personal votes among all candidates, with 18,104. Draško Stanivuković came in second with 15,570. He was appointed Organizational Secretary of the SNSD in February 2024. He graduated from the Faculty of Economics and Management at Bocconi University in Milan.

Zack Polanski backs report endorsing Nato membership and maintaining nuclear weapons
articles.body: Zack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses Britain’s membership of Nato and the maintenance of the country’s nuclear weapons. The Green party leader has welcomed a report from the Verdant thinktank that says the UK should remain in the military alliance and calls for the country to cooperate more closely with France on the maintenance of its nuclear weapons. Party sources stress that its defence policies remain unchanged since 2024, when it went into the last election calling for the UK to sign the UN treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons and immediately begin dismantling its Trident submarines. However, they added that Polanski’s endorsement of the report was part of a debate taking place within the party on how to reassure a broader group of voters on national security issues. Polanski said: “At its core, national security is about food on the table, warm homes and safe communities. That makes it a progressive issue – and I welcome Verdant’s call for a comprehensive security framework that brings people from across the UK into keeping our country safe.” Sacha Deshmukh, the author of the report, said: “Historically some progressives have shied away from recognising security threats. But the right has not been willing to accept the flaws in their policy solutions, so they are not always as strong as they should be – both sides need to change that.” National security has often been seen as one of the Green party’s weak points with a YouGov poll last year showing just 17% of voters trusted the Greens on defence – the lowest of 18 different issues. Concerns over the Greens’ positions on defence have driven some members to call for it to end its opposition to drones and anti-ballistic missiles, something that caused an internal rift ahead of its conference this year. The Verdant report is likely to trigger another round of debate within the party, given that the thinktank, while independent, retains close links to the Greens . The report calls for the government to rethink its national security strategy to focus more on value for money, such as by buying more weapons off the shelf rather than designing high-end bespoke systems for use by the British military. It also calls for more investment in climate adaptation – something some in the green movement view sceptically as taking attention away from efforts to stop the climate deteriorating in the first place. In two policy areas, however, Deshmukh calls for government policy to remain largely the same, despite previous calls from the Green party and Polanski personally for more radical change. On Nato, he calls for the UK to remain a member but push for reform of its structures alongside allies within the alliance. Such a position mirrors the official Green party policy, but contradicts what Polanski has previously said is his personal view. He told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast earlier this year : “Donald Trump has so much domination within Nato that I don’t believe it’s possible to reform Nato from within.” And on the nuclear deterrent, Deshmukh argues the UK could not, and potentially should not, cancel the contract for the next generation of nuclear submarines, known as Dreadnought. However, he adds that the country should seek to cooperate more closely with France on the missiles that will equip it, even though it is being developed to carry the US Trident missiles, which the UK currently uses. Any form of commitment to the nuclear deterrent would be a sharp contrast to the promise the Greens made before the last election, when it said elected members would push for the UK to begin dismantling its nuclear weapons immediately.

articles.title: Trump says he’s inclined to strike Iran after new year if no deal reached
articles.summary: He also accused the regime of stalling negotiations, telling Fox News that "they talk all the time
articles.body: President Trump said he was inclined to resume strikes against Iran after the new year if no deal is reached between Washington and Tehran to end the conflict. Trump acknowledged that indirect talks between the two nations were still ongoing but described Iranian officials as “professional tap dancers.” He also accused the regime of stalling negotiations, telling Fox News that "they talk all the time." "All they do is talk, but it’s all bulls---," the president continued. "They’re more aggressive now than before the election." Trump said he hoped Iran would test the limits of the U.S. military’s naval blockade of nearby ports, because if they did, they'd "all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy.” This comes after Iranian Foreign ​Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters at a weekly press conference that Iran would “use all our tools ​to confront this U.S. aggression,” according to a translation by Reuters. "We will definitely not tolerate ⁠it [the blockade] and we will use all our tools ​to confront this U.S. aggression," Baghaei said. "The naval blockade ... is ​considered a military aggression.” In the past week, Iran and the U.S. have engaged in tit-for-tat attacks as both countries face pressure domestically to end the conflict. The Iranian strikes targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait, while American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday following an unofficial quiet period of roughly two months. Senate Republicans were able to defeat a resolution that would have directed Trump to end hostilities in the Middle East, though the GOP is set to lose its congressional majorities in the new year. Iran is similarly struggling to maintain its war effort as it faces difficulties in financing its attacks due to the economic weight of the U.S. blockade.

articles.title: Ukraine 'keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack,' Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: In the last half hour, Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Nato parliamentary Assembly meeting in Berlin
articles.body:
In the last half hour, Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Nato parliamentary Assembly meeting in Berlin.

He warned that “Russian aggression has shown that when Ukraine is left out, and when there is no clear understanding of how Europe should be protected, anything can happen.”

He also celebrated overnight strikes against Russia, saying Ukraine “keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack.”

“Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refiners are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking.”

Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has repeatedly offered “steps to reduce the fighting,” and “never been the ones to raise the stakes,” but Russia “still gives us no peaceful response.”

He urged Nato leaders to “invest in stronger security and greater resilience,” saying “does anyone here still believe that one day Russia will simply become peaceful and safe again?”

“Just look at the last, last 100 years of Russian history. … There is no reason to believe that Russia will become a different country in one year or five years. So we must act in a way that makes sure that no matter what kind of Russia we face and no matter what threats our countries face, we will always have enough to defend ourselves.”

He urged partners to support Ukraine ahead of winter, particularly helping with air defence systems.

“The stronger our defences are, the less chance Russia has to break through them and the more chance diplomacy has to work.”

The Ukrainian president also slightly pushed back against the suggested Article Five-like security guarantees for Ukraine in case of a peace deal with Russia, arguing that it should simply be allowed to join Nato instead.

“When we talk about Article Five-like guarantees, we need answers. We need answers to some very clear questions. Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again, what exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all these cost and will it really work? All of this is not easy and so far we have no clear, specific answers with respect to such ideas.”

articles.title: Ex-Justice Minister Kang tapped as spy agency chief
articles.summary: He said the changes would bring in new leadership to protect Korea’s interests as the international landscape shifts
articles.body: National Intelligence Service Director nominee Kang Kum-sil / Yonhap President Lee Jae Myung nominated former Justice Minister Kang Kum-sil to head the National Intelligence Service (NIS), Monday. Lee also tapped Lim Woong-soon, his second deputy national security adviser and a former ambassador to Canada, as foreign minister, and Hong Ihk-pyo, a former presidential secretary for political affairs and former floor leader of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), as unification minister. Presidential chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun announced the Cabinet reshuffle largely focused on the security and diplomacy sectors during a briefing at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul. He said the changes would bring in new leadership to protect Korea’s interests as the international landscape shifts. “Kang is the most suitable person to reinforce democratic oversight of the NIS, based on her strong belief in the neutrality of powerful organizations. She is also expected to resolve new security threats, such as cyberattacks, through international cooperation,” the chief of staff said. A former Seoul High Court judge, Kang became Korea’s first female justice minister under the 2003-08 Roh Moo-hyun administration and now serves as ambassador for global climate and environment. If confirmed by the National Assembly, she would be the first woman to lead the spy agency in the history of the NIS and its predecessor agency, founded in 1961. President Lee Jae Myung nominated four Cabinet ministers Monday. From left are Foreign Minister nominee Lim Woong-soon, Unification Minister nominee Hong Ihk-pyo, Interior Minister nominee Han Jun-ho and Culture Minister nominee Kang Yu-jung. Courtesy of Cheong Wa Dae Lim Woong-soon is a career diplomat who served as a minister at the Korean Embassy in Washington and worked on North Korean nuclear issues at the foreign ministry. “Lim Woong-soon is a suitable person to build on Korea-U.S. cooperation based on the ironclad alliance,” the chief of staff said, adding that the foreign minister nominee is expected to expand the horizons of diplomacy from security and trade to industry and advanced technology. Hong, who stepped down as presidential secretary for political affairs earlier this month, previously worked at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and served on the National Assembly’s Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee. The chief of staff said Hong was well placed to lead efforts to ease inter-Korean tensions and rebuild trust. The reshuffle replaced Unification Minister Chung Dong-young and NIS Director Lee Jong-seok, both of whom had prioritized engagement with North Korea but were widely seen as contributing to recent frictions with Washington. There are speculations that the changes are related to fallout from Chung’s March remarks to the National Assembly identifying Kusong as the site of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, after which the U.S. restricted some intelligence sharing on North Korea. At an October parliamentary audit, NIS Director Lee confirmed that Washington had limited information sharing, citing Chung’s disclosure among the factors. As U.S. restrictions on intelligence sharing and visa denials for Korean officials continued, calls grew from both the opposition and within the ruling camp for the two officials to be replaced over their roles in straining the alliance. “The existing policy direction will remain in place,” the chief of staff said when asked whether friction with Washington or questions over the effectiveness of Seoul’s North Korea policy had influenced the reshuffle. Along with the security-related positions, Rep. Han Jun-ho of the DPK was nominated for interior minister, while Kang Yu-jung, the president’s chief spokesperson, was nominated for culture minister. Han, a two-term lawmaker, is a former MBC announcer who served on the DPK’s Supreme Council. Kang Yu-jung worked as a cultural critic and university professor and served on the Assembly’s Culture, Sports, and Tourism Committee before becoming a presidential spokesperson. The education minister position remains vacant after former Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday over confusion surrounding measures to prevent cheating on the national college entrance exam. The chief of staff said the presidential office would move quickly to select a successor.

editorialRejections.body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the decision not to admit Ukraine into NATO in 2008, following a proposal by then-US President George W. Bush, as a “mistake.”Speaking alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at a press conference in Berlin, Friedrich Merz told reporters: "I think we all see today, at least from the point of view of what a mistake it was, not to follow the American proposal in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest."He added that the full-scale invasion of Ukraine would have been 'prevented' had the alliance opened up membership back then."If Ukraine had become a member of NATO, this war would have been likely to be prevented," said Merz, in comments that were translated from German.The meeting came amid ongoing US-led negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, with Rutte visiting the German capital for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly's annual meeting.Rutte struck a cautious tone on the prospect of reviving discussions about Ukraine's NATO membership, stressing that successful peace negotiations would need to come first.The remarks came in response to recent comments by French President Emmanuel Macron, who called for the debate over Ukraine's membership of the alliance to be reopened.Kyiv's potential NATO membership has resurfaced as part of a potential final resolution to ending the war.Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly indicated he would be willing to end the war in Ukraine, provided NATO agrees to return to its 1997 posture. This would effectively mean reversing the alliance's subsequent expansion by withdrawing membership from countries that joined after the collapse of the Soviet Union.However, NATO membership for Ukraine remains a distant prospect, according to Rutte. He noted that while "it's a long-standing position that Ukraine should be a part of NATO," there is no unanimous agreement among alliance members on its accession.Rutte also rebuffed the notion that the Kremlin could have any say in the current or future makeup of the NATO alliance. "What cannot happen is we are forced to roll back NATO to the 1997 borders," he said."It's only the 32 allies deciding who is in NATO and who is not in NATO".Rutte was also addressing ongoing tensions in Europe over increasing Russian hybrid attacks, including last week's incursion into Poland, when two Russian cruise missiles and a drone landed on Polish territory, according to Polish officials.He attributed Russia's increased aggression to mounting battlefield casualties, claiming that Russian forces are losing up to 50,000 soldiers each month in Ukraine. He contrasted this figure with Soviet losses in Afghanistan and US casualties during the Vietnam War."Ukraine is rolling back the frontline in the direction of Russia and striking deep" into Russian territory, Rutte told journalists.Rutte reiterated NATO's position that the best solution to growing hybrid attacks is doubling down on support for Ukraine."Most importantly, we need to keep our military support for Ukraine going," said Rutte."For every incident in Europe - more support for Ukraine," he added.Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the strikes following what he described as “weak meetings” with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.“Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on "X" last Friday.Separately, NATO ambassadors met in Brussels Monday to discuss the Russian incursion into Poland. The alliance is now considering deploying more assets to the region in response.NATO's chief military officer, the Supreme Allied Commander (SACEUR) is now "examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere," a NATO official confirmed to Euronews.

editorialRejections.body: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte reaffirmed alliance support for Moldova's defense and resilience during November 23 talks in Berlin with President Maia Sandu, addressing regional security risks from Russia's war in Ukraine. The two leaders met on the sidelines of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, where Sandu received the Women for Peace and Security award for her contributions to peace, security, and resilience. Both officials reviewed ongoing partnership projects and noted that political dialogue between Chisinau and NATO has reached an advanced stage. Addressing the NATO Parliamentary Assembly plenary, Sandu warned about Russia's information warfare against Moldova, including the use of artificial intelligence. She said electoral interference is prepared well ahead of campaigns through illicit financing networks, propaganda, and efforts to sway public opinion, and called for closer NATO-EU cooperation to counter disinformation. Sandu also highlighted the security spillover from the war in Ukraine. According to figures she presented, Moldovan authorities recorded more than 80 incidents involving drones and other aerial threats in 2026. Rutte urged NATO member states to accelerate defense spending and submit concrete plans to reach at least 5% of GDP by 2035, or sooner. He said threats to European security are real, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage, and drone incursions attributed to Russia. The alliance chief also stressed the need to expand weapons production, air defense, and anti-drone capabilities as demand for military equipment outpaces supply. Moldova's relations with NATO began shortly after independence. The country joined the inaugural meeting of the North Atlantic Cooperation Council in December 1991, entered the Partnership for Peace program in 1994, and established its Mission to NATO in 1997. Chisinau and NATO approved their first Individual Partnership Action Plan (IPAP) in 2006, updating the framework in 2010, 2014, 2017, and 2022. Since 2014, Moldovan troops have participated in NATO's KFOR peacekeeping mission in Kosovo alongside defense capacity-building and interoperability programs. In 2016, both sides signed an agreement to establish the NATO Liaison Office in Chisinau, which officially opened in December 2017.

Olha Bihar, known by her call sign "Vidma," or "Witch," warned that NATO forces are still training their soldiers on traditional military concepts that the battlefield has outgrown, saying drones have fundamentally reshaped war. In an interview with Britain's Forces News in London, Bihar, who heads the Unmanned Systems Directorate of the 20th Army Corps of Ukraine's army, said tanks, armored vehicles and conventional equipment have become almost unable to operate near the front because of the dense presence of drones that can detect and strike targets. She said traditional doctrine and training no longer suit the reality of battle, because drones can destroy classic patterns of fighting and leave soldiers and equipment visible and open to attack around the clock, even when hiding under trees and bushes. Asked whether NATO forces are preparing correctly for future wars, she answered: "No. Definitely not." She called for rethinking military strength, saying "the trend is not about muscles, it's about intellect," and that people armies did not consider fit to fight ten years ago, such as thin young men skilled with computers and video games, are now the ones who can decide the course of battle. She cited the targeting of the Kerch Bridge, which links Crimea to Russia, to show how operations have changed, saying such an operation does not necessarily need a strongly built soldier and "could have been a woman, a skinny gamer, a 50-year-old." Bihar ended by stressing the need to change armies' "frame of thinking" and open up to new ideas in recruitment and training, saying modern wars require technical skills and minds able to handle advanced systems more than traditional physical strength. editorialRejections.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
editorialRejections.summary: The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading
editorialRejections.reason: What explainer headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't. The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders? The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch. Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation". It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism. Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga. Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia. The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers. And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses. It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern". Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar. Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent. If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop? As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe. On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine. It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response. But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants. Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea. In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental. The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war. There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf. Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace. It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives. This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt. There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

editorialRejections.title: Ukraine at UN: Demand for withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Donbas neither compromise nor road to peace
editorialRejections.summary: According to Pavlichenko, the trilateral talks involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Ukraine's Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Volodymyr Pavlichenko said this on Monday at a meeting of the UN Security Council, an Ukrinform correspondent reports. “We need peace, but a comprehensive, just and lasting one, based on the compliance with the principles of the UN Charter and backed by legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine,” the diplomat stressed. According to Pavlichenko, the trilateral talks involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia, which have resumed in Abu Dhabi, should move to the leaders' level, and Kyiv is ready for this. Ukraine had also proposed starting with a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure and at sea in order to protect shipping and global food security. It also supported the US initiative to stop attacks on energy facilities and, accordingly, strikes on Russian oil refineries. He also recalled that on November 19, Putin stated that Russia would no longer discuss a ceasefire covering energy infrastructure and the Black Sea. Pavlichenko emphasized that Ukraine was acting within its right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. “Crimea is Ukraine, and everything on Ukrainian territory is Ukrainian, including the so-called Kerch Bridge. When it comes to what is ours, we have the right to act as we see it,” the diplomat said. He added that Ukraine shared the assessment of U.S. President Donald Trump, who said at a press conference in Washington that Putin was going through difficult times. According to Pavlichenko, Ukraine would continue to increase pressure on Russia. He stressed that Russian terror continued despite Putin's statements about peace, including during his visit to Shenzhen. Moscow is trying to portray itself to the international community as a peacemaker and even a victim, while continuing to attack Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, including energy, transport, food and water facilities. According to Pavlichenko, Russia's demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from Donetsk and Luhansk regions “is not a compromise and is not a road to peace; it would open the road for Russia’s next offensive.” The diplomat stressed that Russia's current territorial gains could not serve as grounds for imposing terms on Ukraine. Pressure on the aggressor must be maintained and intensified, while Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders must be fully restored. “Ukraine has the right to choose its alliances. There can be no limits on our Armed Forces and no imposed neutrality. And no decisions on Ukraine's security can be taken without Ukraine,” the diplomat said. He emphasized that Russia had started the war and could end it at any moment. No complicated peace negotiations or additional formats were needed for this. “Concessions by the victim have never brought peace. Pressure on the aggressor and the strength of the defender will,” Pavlichenko stressed, urging international partners to remain united in their support for Ukraine and to show the same courage as Ukraine. As Ukrinform reported, the UN Security Council, chaired by Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs, convened a high-level meeting on Monday to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine.

editorialRejections.title: Bloodshot eyes and tardiness: When do Kazakh civil servants face drug tests?
editorialRejections.summary: Kazakhstan has approved new rules for identifying signs of drug use among civil servants
editorialRejections.reason: Editor rejected this or a closely matching story
editorialRejections.body: Kazakhstan has approved new rules for identifying signs of drug use among civil servants. Frequent tardiness, bloodshot eyes, drowsiness and even a loss of interest in work can now serve as grounds for referring a government employee for a medical examination. Under the new rules , civil servants’ behavior during working hours will be monitored by their immediate supervisors and human resources departments. They are instructed to look for three categories of signs that may indicate drug use. The third category concerns mental and cognitive changes. These include memory problems, reduced concentration, anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, hallucinations, inconsistent behavior and an inability to critically assess one’s own condition. A single instance of tardiness or bloodshot eyes is not enough to refer a civil servant for a medical examination. Under the order, a referral requires at least three signs of potential drug use from different categories. In such cases, human resources personnel must consider not only the employee’s behavior but also existing information about them, including complaints, performance evaluations, internal memos and other relevant documents. If a supervisor notices suspicious changes in a subordinate’s behavior, they must immediately notify the human resources department. If drug use is confirmed, the head of the government agency must report the findings to the authorized body responsible for civil service affairs and law enforcement agencies. The agency must also consider disciplinary action against the employee. At the same time, civil servants have the right to review their examination results and appeal both the medical conclusion and the actions of government officials. In July 2026, legislative amendments came into force in Kazakhstan requiring drug testing for civil servants. The requirement primarily applies to managers who supervise other employees and civil servants working under special conditions, such as those with access to state secrets. The heads of the respective government agencies are responsible for determining the specific list of positions subject to testing. In March 2026, Kursiv.media also reported on a proposal to classify drug use as conduct that discredits the civil service. Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs was also designated as an offense that could discredit a civil servant. Additionally, in 2024, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law prohibiting civil servants from participating in gambling . The ban reportedly affected approximately 280,000 government officials, military personnel and heads of state-funded organizations. For example, in the North Kazakhstan region, nine officials lost their jobs because of gambling addiction. In the Akmola region, civil servants faced disciplinary action for placing bets worth millions of tenge with bookmakers, while gambling-related offenses in the Zhetysu region also resulted in dismissals.

editorialRejections.title: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate
editorialRejections.summary: But North Macedonia , an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession
editorialRejections.body: The European Union 's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028 , while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms. But North Macedonia , an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession . That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU- Western Balkans summit in Brussels. "The Western Balkans ' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting. North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards. But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan. Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022. For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path. Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow. Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities. The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable. From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework. "It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission 's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast. EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia. Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history : Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people. President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another. "We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said. After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia. A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%. Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward. The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat. The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions. For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks. The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal. According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise. "If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

editorialRejections.title: Albania's Foreign and Defence Ministries deny any role in attack on Russian warship in Libya
editorialRejections.summary: According to media reports, it was carried out by Ukraine's intelligence services
editorialRejections.body: The Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Defence have rejected claims that the drone attack on a Russian warship in Benghazi, Libya, was planned or launched from Albanian territory. The attack happened on Sunday morning. According to media reports, it was carried out by Ukraine's intelligence services. It drew wide attention because it took place far from the front line and in another country, taking the war beyond the borders of Ukraine and Russia. On Sunday evening, a platform that covers military affairs and armed conflicts wrote that the Ukrainian drones had been launched from Albania. That claim pulled Albania into the story, alongside Russia and Ukraine, which have been at war since 2022, and Libya, where the attack took place. In their official responses, both ministries denied any Albanian involvement. They described the reports as inaccurate and not backed by evidence. The Foreign Ministry said the claims that the attack was launched from Albania "do not reflect the facts." "Albania was not involved in this incident, and its territory was not used or made available to launch or support such an attack," the ministry said in a statement. The ministry firmly rejected the accusations. It asked the media and platforms that published them to correct their reports and to stop presenting unverified claims as fact. The Ministry of Defence also denied that Albania's armed forces played any part in the operation. "The Armed Forces of the Republic of Albania did not carry out, take part in, or provide any support for such an operation," it said. The ministry stressed the difference between the fact that an attack happened and the claim that it was launched from Albania. "The fact that an attack took place does not prove where the weapons came from, let alone that Albania was involved," the ministry said. It warned that publishing such claims without independent checks risks spreading a false story linking Albania to a military operation against Russia. A Russian Navy corvette, first identified as the Merkury, caught fire after a powerful explosion at the naval base in Benghazi, in eastern Libya, in the early hours of Sunday, November 22, 2026. The ship has been identified as a Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class missile corvette. According to reports, it had come to Benghazi to take on fuel and supplies as part of cooperation between Russia and the authorities in eastern Libya. Sources quoted by Al Jazeera said there were Russian and Libyan casualties, but gave no confirmed numbers. The ship sank. Photos taken after the incident show only part of it above the water. Witnesses quoted by Al Jazeera said they saw three drones during the night attack. Sources cited by the Associated Press said the drones had been launched from a Ukrainian-controlled base in western Libya. Authorities in Benghazi have opened a joint investigation with Russia. So far they have not directly blamed Ukraine, but they have said that Libya is not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine. At the time of reporting, no one had officially claimed responsibility for the attack. The claim that the attack came from Albania was first published by Clash Report. In a post on X, the platform said that, according to one of its sources, the drones used to hit the Russian warship had been launched from Albania, not from western Libya. The post also claimed that eastern Libyan authorities had identified where the drones were launched from, and that the western Libya story was a cover put out by Ukrainian sources. However, Clash Report did not name its source and did not publish any evidence that the drones came from Albania. According to the Ministry of Defence, the claim was later repeated by another platform, Visioner, which reported that the drones had travelled more than 800 kilometres across the Mediterranean. The ministry said the report was not backed by evidence and warned against repeating it as confirmed fact. Clash Report is a platform that publishes news about military conflicts and international security. It has more than 850,000 followers on X.
